The first time I saw the ocean, I was five years old. My parents took me to a beach in South Carolina, and I stood at the water’s edge, toes sinking into the wet sand, staring at the endless blue horizon. The waves crashed in, relentless and wild, and I remember thinking, *This is bigger than me.* It was the first time I felt both small and connected to something vast.

Years later, I still feel that way when I’m near water. There’s something about its unpredictability—the way it can be calm one moment and furious the next—that reminds me of life itself. You can’t control the ocean, just like you can’t control time or chance. But you can learn to move with it, to find rhythm in its ebb and flow.

I’ve also come to appreciate the quiet moments by the water—the stillness of a lake at dawn, the way fog can turn a familiar shoreline into a dream. There’s a kind of magic in those stillnesses, a reminder that beauty doesn’t always announce itself with fanfare.

Sometimes, when I’m overwhelmed, I close my eyes and imagine the sound of waves. It’s a simple thing, but it grounds me. The ocean doesn’t judge. It doesn’t rush. It just *is*—and in its presence, I remember to breathe.

Maybe that’s why I keep going back. Not because I expect answers, but because the questions themselves feel sacred. The ocean doesn’t give closure; it gives perspective. And sometimes, that’s enough.
